title: Compare the end positions: name the feature that decides
outcomes: Checks the positions two candidates reach on four counts (material, king safety, piece activity, pawn structure) and names the one that differs; the exercises here differ by piece activity and the king's pawn cover
Names the one feature that separates two end positions
Checks what is attacked before trusting a count of squares
Recognises a position where a forcing line, not a comparison, decides

steps.text: After you follow two candidates, **compare the positions they reach**, not the moves. Make four short checks and write one line each: *material, king safety, piece activity (squares the pieces reach), pawn structure.* If material is level, find the **one feature that differs** and say which position it favours. The new step: write the feature's name, not just a preference.

steps.caption: White to move: Qe1 or Qc2, the same queen. Material: level, neither move captures. King cover: pawns on f2, g2, h2 in both. Pawns: a queen move moves none. Activity: Qe1 reaches 14 squares, Qc2 only 7, and the engine prefers Qe1. Careful: Qe3 reaches 15 squares yet the engine rates it more than a pawn below Qe1, so the count alone is not the reason. After Qe3 or Qc2, Black can play ...Qa1+, a check along the first rank, which the four checks do not show.

line.say: Qe1: from here the queen can move to 14 squares. From c2 it would reach 7.

steps.text: **When counting works, and when it fails.** A count of squares helps when material is level and nothing is attacked. If a piece lands where something cheaper attacks it, the count does not matter. It also fails when both moves lead to the same position, or when a forcing line decides and nothing is left to compare. Counting squares is a rule of thumb, not a verdict.

steps.title: Same position, a different second candidate
steps.prompt: Both positions are the same game position. In the first you compare Ne2 with Nd1: the knight reaches more squares from e2. In the second you compare Ne2 with Nd5, where the knight reaches even more. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** Each exercise has three hints. The next four are silent: no hints, no engine. For the first two, write the four checks on paper and name the feature that differs, then answer. The last two ask which tool fits. The plan is to offer hints only on request once you solve unlabeled items without them (planned, not built yet).

steps.prompt: Look at your paper checks for the first two silent positions. This note stays on this device.

steps.text: The next set compares two moves in tactical positions, where one move loses material outright. That is the easy end of the same skill: when the formal counts differ a lot, the comparison is quick. Notice how much of it you did by counting and how much by following a line.

**Two-column sheet: ten minutes, away from the app.** Take two candidates from a position in your own game. Draw two columns and four rows: material, king safety, piece activity, pawn structure. Picture the position after each move and write one line per cell. Circle the row where the columns differ most. Before you trust it, check that no piece stands attacked by something cheaper. Then compare with an engine.
